turns.prompt: Can you explain what chemotherapy does in ordinary language? I am not asking you to choose my treatment.
turns.text:
At its core, chemotherapy uses medicines to target and destroy fast-growing cells. Because cancer cells multiply much faster than most normal cells, chemotherapy works by interrupting their ability to divide, grow, and spread.

Because these medicines travel through your bloodstream, they can reach cancer cells almost anywhere in the body. That is why doctors call chemotherapy a "systemic" treatment.

Some normal, healthy cells also divide quickly—like the cells in your hair follicles, mouth, digestive tract, and bone marrow. Chemotherapy can affect these healthy cells as well, which is what causes common side effects like fatigue, nausea, or hair loss. Healthy cells usually repair themselves once treatment finishes or between cycles.

Depending on your situation, doctors use chemotherapy for different reasons: to shrink a tumour before other treatments, to clean up any remaining cells after surgery, or to control the cancer and ease symptoms if it cannot be completely removed.
